The Defendants argue that the common issues in this case are overwhelmed by the individual issues and that certification is not appropriate when the litigation inevitably will break down into individual proceedings.
In support of this proposition, they cite Controltech Engineering Inc. v.
Ontario Hydro, [1998] O.J.
No.
Gen.
Div.), 1279022 Ontario Ltd. v.
Posen (2004), 184 Man.
R.
C.A.), Kumar v.
Mutual Life Assurance Co. of Canada (2003), 226 D.L.R.
C.A.) and Hollick.
All of these cases were decided on their facts.

The real question is how to determine when individual issues are overwhelming and how to distinguish that situation from cases where individual issues can be managed as expressly contemplated by the CPA.
The relative number of issues in each category provides initial guidance.
Common issues are discussed above and individual issues concern reliance, limitations and damage.
In the case at bar, there are clearly more common issues than individual issues, but that is the starting point only.
Any approach based solely on the number of issues would encourage the drawing up of ever-longer lists of subdivided issues with the hope of tipping a numeric scale.

Rather, the essence of the inquiry is to assess and weigh the nature and significance of the common and individual issues and the impact of the individual issues on the trial process, including fairness to plaintiffs, defendants and the court. … … b)—Limitations The more serious problem for the Plaintiffs is the passage of approximately four years between the closing of the sale of the Lands and the filing of the statement of claim.
This, too, is an individual issue, requiring scrutiny of when class members knew or ought to have known of the factors outlined in s.
3 of the Limitations Act.
The authorities in other jurisdictions appear divided as to whether a limitations defence serves as a bar to certification.
A case in which limitation issues overwhelmed all others was Daniels v.
Canada (Attorney General), [2003] 6 W.W.R.
72 (Sask.
Q.B.), which involved a claim by veterans of World War I, World War II or the Korean War for damages for loss of benefits, negligence, breach of trust, breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment.
The Court refused to certify this class because it was not possible to determine issues of discoverability in any global fashion.
It would have been necessary to have an inquiry into the state of mind of each individual plaintiff over a period of 40 years.
The Court found that all claims had been statute-barred for decades and that a class action would not be “the preferable procedure to determine issues of discoverability”.
That case involved a limitation issue of staggering scope and magnitude: thousands of claimants and forty to sixty years of inquiry.
The range of individual limitations issues raised in the case at bar is nowhere near as far-reaching.

I also note that in Alberta, the issue is not whether a class action would be the preferable procedure concerning discoverability, as stated by the trial judge in Daniels, but whether a class action is the preferable procedure for the fair and efficient of the common issues.
One benefit of a class action is that discovery of the class representative usually will suffice, thus eliminating the need for discovery of each individual plaintiff.
The Supreme Court stated in Dutton at para.
59 that “Cases where individual discovery is required of all class members are the exception rather than the rule.
Indeed, the necessity of individual discovery may be a factor weighing against allowing the action to proceed in representative form.” S.
18 of the CPA specifically contemplates that a defendant may seek leave to conduct individual discoveries of class members; s.
18(4) then requires that consideration be given to whether individual discovery is necessary in view of the defences of the party seeking leave. ….

The presence of a triable limitation defence may challenge the bifurcated process because it superimposes individual determinations on an issue which, if resolved in favour of the Defendants, operates as a defence providing immunity.
It may require the discovery of class members.
It is possible that it will create individual inquires, but this is not a case like Mouhteros where, at para.
31, the court stated that “what common issues there may be are completely subsumed by the plethora of individual issues, which would necessitate individual trial for virtually each class member”.

In this case, the limitations issue may play a role in the ultimate determination of liability; however, given the common elements in the circumstances of this case, I am of the view that it plays a less significant role in comparison with the resolution of the common issues.
Although there are individual issues concerning reliance and limitations there is utility, fariness and efficiency in deciding the common issues in a class proceeding.
The origin of the obligations and entitlement, if any, are the same.
There are important factual issues shared by all Investors and there is no utility in building the same factual foundation more than once.
In my view, individual issues do not predominate over or overwhelm the common issues. … (C)—s.
5(2)(d): Other means of resolving the claims S.
5(2)(d) of the CPA requires the Court to consider whether other means of resolving the claims are less practical or less efficient.
Alternate procedures available to the class members could include:
(1) multiple separate actions
(2) multiple actions consolidated and tried together; or
(3) a test case, which could lead to further actions by those who choose to bring them if the Plaintiffs were successful. … (D)—s.
5(2)(e): Administration of the class proceedings The CPA specifically contemplates resolution of both common and individual issues.
S.
12 outlines the stages of class proceedings and provides that common issues are to be determined together and individual issues are to be determined according to ss.
The Court may give separate judgment in respect of these different sets of issues.
In light of this, I do not see how the administration of a class proceeding would create greater difficulties than those likely to be experienced if relief were sought by other means. … (v)—s.
5(1)(e): Representative plaintiff Finally, s.
5(1)(e) of the CPA deals with the appointment of a representative plaintiff and sets out three requirements.

First, the representative plaintiff must, in the opinion of the Court, fairly and adequately represent the interests of the class. … Second, the proposed representative plaintiffs must have produced a plan for proceeding that sets out a workable method of notice and advancing the action. … Third, there must be no conflict of interest between the prospective representative plaintiff and other prospective class members. … Madam Justice Martin provided a further overview of the “statutory framework and general principles” in Andriuk v.
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2013 ABQB 422, 2013 CarswellAlta 1492.
In Windsor v.
Canadian Pacific Railway (2006), 402 A.R.
162 (Alta.
Q.B.); varied 2007 ABCA 294, 2007 CarswellAlta 1262, 417 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 244, Rooke J. gave the following summary of applicable principles (at pp.
162]): 67 The few certification decisions under the Act to date have provided lengthy legal summaries and analyses, establishing inter alia the following principles:

(a) the Act requires a purposive approach and provides extensive flexibility to the certification justice to deal with the proceedings as they unfold, such as decertifying the proceedings or common issues later on if need be: Ayrton—Appeal, at para.
14; (b) if it appears on the face of the proceeding that the Action is doomed to fail, then there is little point in certifying the Action: T.L., at para.
36; (c) class definitions must not be merits-based in that inclusion should not depend upon the outcome of the Action—this is a circular definition that is to be avoided: T.L., at para.
80; (d) exclusion of some persons similarly situated to potential class members might be appropriate if doing so makes the class proceeding more manageable: T.L., at para.

(e) as the Act requires a certification application within a prescribed time, the absence of a Statement of Defence does not prevent the determination of what the common issues are—such determination will be made with regard to the pleadings and evidence available: Condominium Plan No.
Investplan Properties Inc., [2006] A.J.
No.
368, 2006 ABQB 224, at para.
Martin J.); (f) an issue central to class members' claims, which, when determined will advance the class members' claims in a meaningful way, will be a common issue: Ayrton v.
PRL Financial (Alta.) Ltd.
L.R.
(4th) 106, 2005 ABQB 311 (LoVecchio J.) (“Ayrton—Motion”), at para.
84-85, aff'd in Ayrton—Appeal

(g) even where individual issues might predominate in the sense that much work will remain after resolution of the common issues, there might still be practical utility in deciding the common issues once, even if the overall benefits are slight: T.L., at para.

133; (h) whether a class proceeding is the “preferable” procedure is a question of law to be determined by the certification justice based on his or her knowledge of the Court's processes: T.L., at para.

30; (i) while evidence of widespread complaints within a proposed class regarding the Defendant's conduct may assist the certification analysis, such evidence is not required by the Act: Kristal Inc. v.
Nicholl and Akers, [2006] A.J.
No.
Martin J.), at para.
138; (j) the ability of a representative plaintiff meeting a costs award is a relevant factor, but not an absolute bar to certification: T.L., at para.
122; (k) a “sparse” litigation plan may still be sufficient for the purposes of certification: Condominium Plan No.
0020701, at para.

(l) a representative plaintiff may be appointed, even if he or she is not a member of the proposed class, if to do so would avoid a substantial injustice and if an individual is put forward who can be discovered on matters relating to the class: Condominium Plan No.
0020701, at para.
(b) Common interest In Paron v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection), 2006 ABQB 375, 2006 CarswellAlta 619, 402 A.R.
85, 60 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 95, Topolniski, J., at pp.

116-118, said: Section 5(1)(c) requires that the claims of the prospective class members raise a common issue, whether or not the common issue predominates over issues affecting only individual prospective class members.
A common issue means common, but not necessarily identical, issues of fact or law that arise from common, but not necessarily, identical facts.
There must be some evidence presented to support each common issue: Hollick (at para.
An issue is common if its resolution is necessary to the resolution of each class member's claim.
As such, it must be a substantial ingredient of each of the class members' claims, and resolution of the issue must materially advance the litigation.
Something may be a substantial ingredient of the claim even if it makes up a limited aspect of the liability question and even though many individual issues remain to be decided after its resolution.

The latter does not undermine the commonality conclusion, but is a factor on the assessment of whether a class action is the “preferable procedure.” Success for one class member must mean success for all; all members of the class must benefit from the successful prosecution of the action, although not necessarily to the same extent.
If one class member is successful on a common issue, either all class members are successful or some class members are indifferent to that issue.
There is no common issue, if success for one member of the class means loss for another.

In Metera, Slatter J described the real focus of this analysis as being whether there is a conflict of interest within the class, observing that such conflicts tend to destroy the commonality of interest and put counsel in an impossible situation.
In some cases a conflict of interest can be dealt with by naming formal subclasses, and if necessary providing for separate representation for each of the subclasses.
Alternatively, the problem can be resolved by redefining the class to exclude those with conflicting interests.

However, in other instances the conflict may be so fundamental that it prevents the action from proceeding as a class action, for example, where all the issues are only “sub-class common” and there are no “universally common issues.” The assessment of the common issues is contextual, in light of all the issues raised by the case, and caution must be exercised to ensure that the issues are truly common, not just made to appear common by the manner in which they are posed.
As noted by Cullity J. in Joanisse v.

Barker: As drafted, the proposed issues have an appearance of commonality in the sense that an affirmative, or negative, answer to the question posed by each of them would resolve the issue in respect of all members of the class.
In that sense, the task of framing common issues for the purpose of a motion for certification would rarely, if ever, give rise to difficulty.
In most cases, the question whether the defendants are liable to the members of the class could be considered to be a common issue.
If that were sufficient, the requirement of commonality would call for nothing more than an exercise in drafting.

If, on the pleading and evidentiary record, the conclusion is that an issue would have to be decided separately in the light of the particular circumstances of each member, certification on the basis of such an issue is not justified.

This is so whether the defect is to be understood as detracting from the commonality of the issue, or as affecting the question of the preferable procedure to be determined under section 5(1)(d) of the CPA.
While the Plaintiffs need not show that everyone in the class shares the same interest in the resolution of a common issue, there must be some showing that the class is not unnecessarily broad.
In other words, they must show that the class could not be defined more narrowly without arbitrarily excluding some people who share the same interest in the resolution of the common issue.
If the class is capable of more narrow definition, certification should either be disallowed or allowed on condition that the definition is narrowed.

It does not serve the ends of either fairness or efficiency to certify an action on the basis of issues that are common only when stated in the most general terms, because inevitably such action will break down into individual proceedings.
(c) When is a class proceeding the preferable procedure?
In Paron v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection), 2006 ABQB 375, 2006 CarswellAlta 619, 402 A.R.
85, 60 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 95, Topolniski, J., at pp.

123-124, said: A class proceeding is the preferable procedure if it presents a fair, efficient and manageable method of determining common issues, and if such determinations will advance the proceeding in accordance with the goals of judicial economy, access to justice, and behaviour modification.

The essence of the inquiry is to assess the common and individual issues contextually, and consider the impact of the individual issues on the trial process, including fairness to plaintiffs, defendants and the court.
It focuses on two questions:
(1) would the class action be a fair, efficient and manageable method of advancing the claim
(2) would the class action be preferable to all other reasonably available means of resolving the claims of class members.
(d) Costs Against Representative Plaintiff In Ayrton v.
PRL Financial (Alta.) Ltd., 2006 ABCA 88, 2006 CarswellAlta 319, 384 A.R.
1, 57 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 1, the Court said, at p.

10: …in Alberta, class action litigants can only avoid the risk of costs to be paid by a representative plaintiff by applying for an order for no costs in the proceedings and relying upon common law principles for public interest litigation.
There is nothing in the Class Proceedings Act that expressly prohibits such an order.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.8 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 1)
paragraphs.text: (1) If under section 18(2) of the Class Proceedings Act the Court requires a class member or subclass member to file and serve an affidavit of records, the Court may do either or both of the following: (a) limit the purpose and scope of the records to be produced and of questioning; (b) determine how the evidence obtained may be used. (2) If a class member or subclass member is questioned under section 18(2) of the Class Proceedings Act, the Court may do either or both of the following: (a) limit the purpose and scope of the questioning; (b) determine how the evidence obtained may be used.
